claim: A count noun denotes individuals which cannot divide into smaller things of the same kind.
evidence_summary: “We divided an interval into three shorter intervals” (constructed). The article an and the numeral three with a plural independently mark the two count uses. The original interval and each of its three proper parts satisfy the same noun in the same mathematical sense.
finding: Counting requires a unit at the chosen level of description. It does not require a unit with no interval as a proper part. Conversely, people may count pieces to judge how much furniture there is (CG-0005).
proposed_wording: A count use presents entities as units relative to a context. An interval may count as one unit even when it contains shorter intervals. Use the distribution with numerals and determiners to identify count syntax.
inference: Must a count individual lack proper parts that also satisfy the same noun?

evidence.source: OpenStax, Calculus Volume 2. Chapter 1, Key Terms.
evidence.passage: §3.1, p. 335, paragraph after [5]. Having defined a count use through individuals and illustrated boy, CGEL says they “cannot be divided into smaller parts of the same kind as the whole”.
evidence.example: A partition divides an interval into subintervals. Each subinterval is an interval in the same mathematical sense. The example with an and three shorter intervals is constructed in this audit.
evidence.establishes: The source establishes the part–whole relation. In the constructed sentence the article and the low cardinal independently establish the count distribution.
evidence.locator: Entries for partition and regular partition.

evidence.source: Susan Rothstein (2010). Counting and the mass/count distinction. Journal of Semantics 27(3), 343–397.

evidence.example: The discussion asks what counts as one fence in a context and compares other count nouns with same-kind parts.
evidence.establishes: Published precedent for context-sensitive counting units. Interval is the catalogue’s extension of the argument.

evidence.source: David Barner & Jesse Snedeker (2005). Quantity judgments and individuation: Evidence that mass nouns count. Cognition 97(1), 41–66.
evidence.passage: §3.1, p. 335, paragraph after [5]. Having defined a count use through individuals and illustrated boy, CGEL says they “cannot be divided into smaller parts of the same kind as the whole”.
evidence.example: Participants could judge the quantity of a non-count noun for discrete objects, such as furniture, by the number of objects, even when the competing set contained larger objects.
evidence.establishes: Number-based judgments can accompany non-count syntax. This bears directly on the converse of the proposed count-noun condition.
evidence.locator: Experiments comparing quantity judgments for object-mass, count and substance nouns.
